title: History of Hinduism
wiki_lead:
The history of Hinduism covers a wide variety of related religious traditions native to the Indian subcontinent. It overlaps or coincides with the development of religion in the Indian subcontinent since the Iron Age, with some of its elements possibly tracing back to prehistoric religions such as those of the Bronze Age Indus Valley Civilisation. Hinduism has been called the "oldest religion" in the world, but scholars regard Hinduism as a relatively recent synthesis of various Indian cultures and traditions, with diverse roots and no single founder, which emerged around the beginning of the Common Era.
The history of Hinduism is often divided into periods of development. The first period is the pre-Vedic period, which includes the Indus Valley Civilization and local pre-historic religions. Northern India had the Vedic period with the introduction of the historical Vedic religion by the Indo-Aryan migrations, starting somewhere between 1900 BCE and 1400 BCE. The subsequent period of the second urbanisation (600–200 BCE) is a formative period for Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism followed by "a turning point between the Vedic religion and Hindu religions," during the Epic and Early Puranic period (c. 200 BCE to 500 CE), when the Epics and the first Purānas were composed. This was followed by the classical "Golden Age" of Hinduism (c. 320–650 CE), which coincides with the Gupta Empire. In this period the six branches of Hindu philosophy evolved, namely, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mīmāṃsā, and Vedānta. Monotheistic sects like Shaivism and Vaishnavism developed during this same period through the Bhakti movement. It flourished in the  medieval period  from roughly 650 to 1100 CE, which forms the late Classical period or early Middle Ages, 
with the decline of Buddhism in India and the establishment of classical Puranic Hinduism.
Hinduism under both Hindu and Islamic rulers from c. 1200 to 1750 CE saw the increasing prominence of the Bhakti movement, which remains influential today. Adi Shankara became glorified as the main proponent of Advaita Vedanta, in response to the success of Vaishnavite bhakti.
The colonial period saw the emergence of various Hindu reform movements partly inspired by western movements, such as Unitarianism and Theosophy. The Partition of India in 1947 was along religious lines, with the Republic of India emerging with a Hindu majority. During the 20th century, due to the Indian diaspora, Hindu minorities have formed in all continents, with the largest communities in absolute numbers in the United States and the United Kingdom.

Roots of Hinduism
While the Puranic chronology presents a genealogy of thousands of years, scholars regard Hinduism as a fusion, synthesis, or amalgamation of various Indian cultures and traditions.
Among its roots are the historical Vedic religion, itself already the product of "a composite of the Indo-Aryan and Harappan cultures and civilizations", which evolved into the Brahmanical religion and ideology of the Kuru kingdom of Iron Age northern India; but also the Śramaṇa or renouncer traditions of northeast India, and mesolithic and neolithic cultures of India, such as the religions of the Indus Valley Civilisation, Dravidian traditions, and the local traditions and tribal religions.
This Hindu synthesis emerged after the Vedic period, between 500–200 BCE and c. 300 CE, in the period of the second urbanisation and the early classical period of Hinduism, when the Epics and the first Puranas were composed. This Brahmanical synthesis incorporated śramaṇic and Buddhist influences and the emerging bhakti tradition into the Brahmanical fold via the smriti literature. This synthesis emerged under the pressure of the success of Buddhism and Jainism, starting with the conquest of the Vedic heartland by the Nanda and Maurya rulers, which deprived the Brahmins of their patrons, threatening the survival of the Vedic ritual tradition. grok_lead: The history of Hinduism chronicles the emergence and transformation of religious traditions in the Indian subcontinent, integrating possible pre-Vedic elements from the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2500â1500 BCE) with the Vedic culture introduced by Indo-Aryan migrations from the PonticâCaspian steppe around 2000â1500 BCE, as corroborated by genetic evidence of Steppe ancestry admixture in ancient Indian subcontinental populations. Linguistic and genetic data, including evidence from the Indo-Aryan Mitanni kingdom's treaties (c. 1500â1300 BCE) invoking Vedic deities such as Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatyas, further support waves of Indo-Aryan migrations and the composite development of Hinduism against claims of purely indigenous continuity. This synthesis formed the basis of early Vedic religion, documented in the four Vedas â Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda âcomposed orally between c. 1500 and 500 BCE. These texts emphasize sacrificial rituals, hymns to deities like Indra and Agni, and nascent cosmological speculations. From the late Vedic period onward, ritual orthodoxy evolved into philosophical inquiry through the Upanishads (c. 800â200 BCE) and Brahmanas, articulating core concepts such as dharma (cosmic order), karma (action and consequence), samsara (cycle of rebirth), and moksha (liberation). These underpin Hinduism's six orthodox darshanas including Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Sankhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta. The classical era (c. 200 BCEâ500 CE) witnessed the compilation of epics like the Mahabharata (including the Bhagavad Gita) and Ramayana, alongside Puranas that popularized sectarian worship of Vishnu, Shiva, and Devi. This fostered temple architectures and bhakti devotion amid interactions with Buddhism and Jainism following the Shunga Empire's (c. 185â73 BCE) revival of Vedic rituals and opposition to heterodoxies. Maritime expansions to Southeast Asia influenced Hinduized kingdoms such as Funan (1stâ6th centuries CE), Chenla (6thâ8th centuries CE), Champa (2ndâ15th centuries CE), and the Mataram Kingdom (8thâ10th centuries CE). Medieval developments from c. 500â1500 CE featured patronage by Hindu dynasties such as the Pallavas (c. 275â897 CE), Rashtrakutas (c. 753â982 CE), Gurjara-Pratiharas (c. 730â1036 CE), Kakatiya dynasty (c. 1163â1323 CE) noted for Rudrama Devi as one of the earliest prominent Hindu female rulers and resistance to Islamic invasions from the Delhi Sultanate, Hoysalas (c. 1026â1343 CE), and Gajapatis (c. 1434â1541 CE) who resisted Islamic invasions in Odisha and parts of eastern India. These and the Hindu Shahis (c. 843â1026 CE) in Afghanistan and northwest India constructed rock-cut and structural temples dedicated to deities like Shiva and Vishnu, including sites with Sanskrit inscriptions and artifacts such as the 7thâ8th century marble statue of Surya from Khair Khaneh near Kabul. Southern and eastern areas proved more recalcitrant, with the Rutbils (Zunbils) of Zabulistan, who practiced Hinduism with a large Hindu temple located in Sakawand as a notable center of their pre-Islamic faith (centered in modern southern Afghanistan), mounting repeated defenses, including alliances with Indian kingdoms, repelling Arab incursions until defeats in the 690s CE under governors like Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Bakra, though full submission required ongoing punitive expeditions into the 8th century. The Khmer Empire (9thâ15th centuries CE) and the Majapahit Empire (13thâ16th centuries CE) continued these Hindu-Buddhist traditions in Southeast Asia. Regional bhakti movements emphasizing personal devotion over ritual, along with vernacular poetry by saints like Kabir and Mirabai, developed as a cultural revival. Both adaptations and resistance under Islamic rule included Raja Ganesha's establishment of Hindu rule in Bengal (c. 1414 CE), Mewar Rajputs under Rana Kumbha, Maharana Hammir Singh, Rana Sanga, and Maharana Pratap who resisted Islamic forces, the Vijayanagara Empire's (c. 1336â1646 CE) promotion of Hindu culture and defense against Islamic invasions, the Maratha Empire's (c. 1674â1818 CE) assertion of Hindu swaraj, Hindu ruler Hemu, who won 22 battles against Afghan rebels and Mughal forces (1553â1556 CE), and Pratapaditya's resistance in Jessore (early 17th century). Hindu maritime trade also extended merchant communities to sites like the Ateshgah Fire Temple in Baku featuring Sanskrit inscriptions (17thâ19th centuries CE). The colonial period (18thâ20th centuries) spurred reformist responses from figures like Ram Mohan Roy and Swami Vivekananda, who promoted monotheistic interpretations and global outreach, and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820â1891), who championed widow remarriage, women's education, and opposition to child marriage. Post-independence India saw constitutional secularism alongside Hindu nationalism, with Hinduism's traditions influencing over a billion adherents worldwide through migration and cultural exchange. Hinduism's resilience lies in its composite, decentralized, adaptive structure without a single founder or creed, whose expansive narrative, philosophical and legal traditions have shaped much of Asia.
